raw_case_text:
We diagnosed the first case of disseminated-CL in Ecuador and named it as "generalized CL". The patient was a 40-year-old female, as of the time of examination (August 1979). The patient came from a small village, Balao Chico, Guayas province, a mountainous area located at 200 m a.s.l. (Fig. 1 (2)). At the early phase of the disease, the lesion appeared on the lumbar region, and then papular lesions were seen, which became pustulous vesicles at the right lumber region and disseminated all over the body, demonstrating 308 generalized lesions counted. The patient revealed a marked right lumbar pain, and some of the lesions in the body surface suspecting herpes zoster were observed. The patient was admitted for 16 days in a private hospital and then was taken to a national hospital "Hospital Luis Vernaza" in Guayaquil city, Ecuador. She was admitted to the hospital under the suspected diagnosis of smallpox, being registered No. 03739 in August 1979, without a precise diagnosis. As there was no improvement of her lesions on the 15th day of admission, she was taken to receive differential diagnosis at the National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, Guayaquil city, Ecuador. The presumptive clinical diagnoses were paracoccidioidomycosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, or staphylococcal infections. Firstly, the case was considered as paracoccidioidomycosis suggesting a generalized cutaneous form of the disease. But either Paracoccidioides braziliensis or Staphylococcus aureus were not observed in the examination of ulcer materials. Laboratory examinations revealed positive for betahemolytic streptococcus and sensitive for erythromycin, cephalexin, amikacin, and ampicillin and stool examination positive for Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Ancylostoma duodenale.
Most of the ulcer was crusty. When lifting the crusts, they were excavated with a purulent fluid because of sever secondary infections. The ulcers had different sizes ranging from 0.5 to 20 mm in diameter. Some lesions had thick, prominent, and adhered crusts that bleed easily when they were separated. Others were small crusty ulcers that left an excavation, and some of them were erythematous and papulous, and confluent plaques were found on the lumbar-dorsal region. Several smear samples from diverse regions of the body surface were taken at random. The samples were positive for the Leishmania amastigote, though the number was scanty in smear specimens. The parasite isolated was identified as L. (V.) panamensis (designated as MHOM/EC/95/NA-03) by ELISA species-specific monoclonal antibodies (serodeme) analysis. No Montenegro skin test and rK39 kit test were performed in the case. The patient responded well to Glucantime  treatment (6.5 mg/kg/day for 12 days). In this case, both metronidazole per os and its ointment were also used as a supplementary treatment; probably, these accelerated the patient's healing within a short regimen, in spite of a relatively low dose of the drug.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old female presented with severe right lumbar pain and extensive disseminated pustulovesicular and crusted skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 40-year-old female presented in August 1979 with acute-onset right lumbar pain followed by an initial lumbar skin lesion. The eruption progressed rapidly into papules and pustular vesicles on the right flank, subsequently disseminating over the entire body, totaling 308 lesions. She was hospitalized for 16 days in a private clinic and transferred to Hospital Luis Vernaza under suspicion of smallpox (reg. No. 03739). Lacking improvement by day 15 of admission, she was referred to the National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in Guayaquil for differential diagnosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Balao Chico, Guayas province, Ecuador (mountainous area at 200 m a.s.l.). Prior medical conditions and prior antibiotic therapy not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe right lumbar pain, widespread ulcerative skin eruptions. Denied systemic fever, chills, cough, or gastrointestinal bleeding.

objective.physical_examination: Total of 308 disseminated cutaneous lesions counted over the entire body surface. Erythematous, papular, and confluent plaques on the lumbodorsal region. Lesions ranged from 0.5 to 20 mm in diameter; most were crusted, and removal of crusts revealed excavated ulcers with purulent exudate due to secondary bacterial infection; some crusts were thick, prominent, and bled easily on separation.
objective.routine_investigations: Ulcer exudate culture grew beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (sensitive to erythromycin, cephalexin, amikacin, and ampicillin); negative for Staphylococcus aureus and Paracoccidioides braziliensis. Stool microscopy revealed Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Ancylostoma duodenale.
objective.advanced_workup: Multiple random skin lesion smears stained with Giemsa: light microscopy revealed intracellular microorganisms within phagocytes, present in scanty numbers.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis (generalized CL) caused by Leishmania (Viannia) panamensis, complicated by secondary beta-hemolytic streptococcal pyoderma and intestinal helminthiasis.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Direct smear specimens revealed Leishmania amastigotes. Parasite isolate (MHOM/EC/95/NA-03) identified as Leishmania (Viannia) panamensis by ELISA species-specific monoclonal antibodies (serodeme analysis). Montenegro skin test and rK39 test were not performed.
Differentials Ruled Out: Smallpox (initial hospital misdiagnosis), herpes zoster, paracoccidioidomycosis, and primary staphylococcal ecthyma.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Secondary streptococcal infection treated with sensitive antibiotics. Antileishmanial therapy administered with intramuscular meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime) at 6.5 mg/kg/day for 12 days, supplemented with oral and topical metronidazole. The patient responded rapidly and achieved complete healing of all 308 lesions.
